hits.draft_en:
One day after launch, Claude Fable 5.2 beat a motion studio to a client job.

The studio wanted $6,800 and 3 weeks for a 45-second launch film. The counter-pitch: $2,400, delivered in a day. It actually took 9 hours, cost nothing beyond the $200 plan, and the money arrived that same night. 34x cheaper, 56x faster.

The whole video workflow sits on 8 free repos:
- Real-ESRGAN: 4K upscale, so the draft is already the final master
- Depth Anything V2: adds depth to a still image so the camera can fly through
- RIFE: frame interpolation, choppy 24fps becomes fluid 60fps
- TDMCP: TouchDesigner's own server for node graphs and GLSL shader code, verifying every output
- color-grade-ai: diagnoses a frame and exports a .cube LUT ready for Premiere or Resolve
- rive-mcp: character rigging for Rive - skeletons, easing curves, state logic - no editor
- Kdenlive MCP: edits the full cut in Kdenlive including captions and render
- open-fusion-mcp: kinetic typography and multi-scene comps you can still edit in DaVinci Resolve Fusion

The film went to the client. The pipeline is free for anyone to copy - full repo walkthrough below.

Fable ships with hardened cybersecurity and biology safeguards. That is the leash. It blocks certain classes of work and re-routes flagged requests to Opus automatically.

AI can build your app in a weekend. Hackers can break it in minutes.

Vibe coding has made software development faster, but speed often comes at the expense of security.

This guide identifies 20 common vulnerabilities in AI-built apps and provides a Claude Code prompt to audit and fix them.

The biggest risks include:

→ Exposed secrets: API keys and .env files accidentally pushed to GitHub.

→ Broken access controls: Users accessing other people's data through predictable IDs or missing ownership checks.

→ SQL injection: Unsafe queries that let attackers manipulate database operations.

→ Weak authentication: Plaintext passwords, insecure token storage, and missing email verification.

→ Unprotected endpoints: No rate limits, unchecked webhooks, or unrestricted file uploads.

→ Poor production hygiene: Exposed stack traces and outdated dependencies with known vulnerabilities.

The article provides a full 20-point audit prompt for Claude Code.

It instructs the agent to:

→Find each vulnerability and identify its location.
→Fix issues it can safely resolve.
→Explain anything requiring human decisions.
→Summarize remaining risks before deployment.

If you can only prioritize five, start with exposed secrets, disabled row-level security, predictable IDs without ownership checks, SQL injection, and weak password storage.

The bigger alpha: Building an app with AI is becoming easier. Knowing how to secure what AI builds is becoming a valuable skill.

Run the audit before your next deployment, not after your first breach.

Read the full guide below and copy the audit prompt into Claude Code.

Same 12 coding tasks: Codex read 168K tokens, Claude Code 53K.

@BobEUnlimited's 190K-view post says token usage at OpenAI and Anthropic is slipping. So we checked what one small coding task actually burns: Codex with GPT-6.1 Terra against Claude Code with Opus 5.5, 6 tasks, 2 runs each, hidden tests.

→ Tasks passed: Codex 12 of 12, Claude Code 12 of 12
→ Median input tokens per task: Codex 168.7K, Claude Code 52.9K (3.2x)
→ Median time: Codex 34 s, Claude Code 14 s

The twist: we also ran both at low effort, and it barely changed the input. Codex read 168.7K at medium and 168.7K at low, Claude Code 53.5K and 52.9K. The cost sits in the context each agent carries into every turn, not in the thinking.

How many tokens does your agent read before it touches your first file?

Repost this now, because most people turn the effort knob down to save tokens and it leaves the biggest number where it was.

Follow @stas_sorokin_ for numbers from AI systems running in real production.

Grok Bot is now officially out of beta. The Grok Bot account announced it as AI teammates that work alongside your whole team. - Beta launch: Aug 11, 2026

- Launch post: 12K views on the follow-up, Musk's repost 577K views

AI can build your app in a weekend. Hackers can break it in minutes.

Vibe coding has made software development faster, but speed often comes at the expense of security.

This guide identifies 20 common vulnerabilities in AI-built apps and provides a Claude Code prompt to audit and fix them.

The biggest risks include:

→ Exposed secrets: API keys and .env files accidentally pushed to GitHub.

→ Broken access controls: Users accessing other people's data through predictable IDs or missing ownership checks.

→ SQL injection: Unsafe queries that let attackers manipulate database operations.

→ Weak authentication: Plaintext passwords, insecure token storage, and missing email verification.

→ Unprotected endpoints: No rate limits, unchecked webhooks, or unrestricted file uploads.

→ Poor production hygiene: Exposed stack traces and outdated dependencies with known vulnerabilities.

The article provides a full 20-point audit prompt for Claude Code.

It instructs the agent to:

→Find each vulnerability and identify its location.
→Fix issues it can safely resolve.
→Explain anything requiring human decisions.
→Summarize remaining risks before deployment.

If you can only prioritize five, start with exposed secrets, disabled row-level security, predictable IDs without ownership checks, SQL injection, and weak password storage.

The bigger alpha: Building an app with AI is becoming easier. Knowing how to secure what AI builds is becoming a valuable skill.

Run the audit before your next deployment, not after your first breach.

Read the full guide below and copy the audit prompt into Claude Code.

Same 12 coding tasks: Codex read 168K tokens, Claude Code 53K.

@BobEUnlimited's 190K-view post says token usage at OpenAI and Anthropic is slipping. So we checked what one small coding task actually burns: Codex with GPT-6.1 Terra against Claude Code with Opus 5.5, 6 tasks, 2 runs each, hidden tests.

→ Tasks passed: Codex 12 of 12, Claude Code 12 of 12

How many tokens does your agent read before it touches your first file?

Repost this now, because most people turn the effort knob down to save tokens and it leaves the biggest number where it was.

Grok Bot 1.0 just launched with shareable team AI teammates today. Here's what you need to know.

Grok Bot is now officially out of beta. The Grok Bot account announced it as AI teammates that work alongside your whole team. Elon Musk reposted it and wrote: "Hire Grok Bot as a colleague and give it your hardest tasks!" Reports credit the launch to SpaceX, and the blog post is on

The big change is multiplayer. You can share Bots, work with them in Slack and Teams, and invite them to meetings and video calls. xAI says Bots learn as they work and get more helpful over time.

This is built on Team Bots. One owner sets up a Bot once with apps, secrets, skills and files. They then share it with the whole team or with chosen people, so everyone works from the same context.

A new safety feature came with it. If a web page or message tries to slip hidden instructions into your chat, the bot shows a warning and does not follow them.

xAI says it already uses Bots as teammates that own outcomes across accounting, support, sales and marketing. Rollout to Ultra, Team and Enterprise users runs throughout today.

This follows the iMessage update we covered earlier. Grok Bot began as a beta on Aug 11, 2026, with a 14-day free trial and then $200 a month standalone. Reports say it is also included in SuperGrok Heavy, and that it later started at $30 a month inside the X Subscription.

How Skill Recorder works:
1. Hit record (⌘⇧R or Ctrl+Shift+R) and do the task normally. You can talk through it out loud too.
2. It captures your clicks, app switches, pages and terminal commands, all on your machine.
3. GitHub Copilot turns the recording into a list of steps you can edit.
4. One click turns it into a skill your agent can run, or an automation on a schedule.

It generalizes from one example, so recording yourself submitting one form teaches the agent to submit all of them.
